topics.name: 1 · Drug Toxicity and Poisoning
topics.notes: Therapeutic index = TD50/ED50. Margin of safety = LD1/ED99. Toxicity types: dose-dependent, allergic, idiosyncratic, drug-drug interaction. Poisoning care: ABCDE, stop exposure, decontaminate, give the antidote.

questions.q: How is the therapeutic index (TI) computed?
questions.explain: TI = TD50/ED50. With ED50 = 2 and TD50 = 6, TI = 3.

questions.q: Margin of safety is computed as:
questions.explain: It uses ED99 for the desired effect and LD1 for the undesired effect.

questions.q: Drug A has LD1/ED99 = 1 and Drug B has 0.0002. Which is safer?
options: Drug B, because its value is smaller
Drug A, because its margin of safety is larger
questions.explain: A larger margin of safety means a safer drug, so Drug B is much less safe.

questions.q: Which statement about the therapeutic index is true?
options: It compares the toxic dose to the effective dose in 50% of individuals
questions.explain: TI uses TD50 over ED50 from the quantal dose-response curve.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four types of therapeutic drug toxicity?
questions.explain: The four types are dose-dependent, allergic, idiosyncratic and drug-drug interactions.

questions.q: In dose-dependent reactions, toxicity is proportional to:
options: Drug concentration in the body and duration of exposure
questions.explain: Both concentration and duration of exposure matter.

questions.q: CNS depression from barbiturates (sedation to coma to death) is an example of:
questions.explain: It is dose-dependent: the higher the barbiturate dose, the deeper the depression.

questions.q: Tardive dyskinesia from antipsychotics depends mainly on:
questions.explain: It appears after months to years of use.

questions.q: Which drug class is a classic cause of phototoxicity?
questions.explain: Tetracyclines are the phototoxicity example in the lecture.

questions.q: Which extrapyramidal reaction appears first (hours to 5 days)?
questions.explain: Dystonia: hours to 5 days. Parkinsonism: 5-30 days. Akathisia: 5-60 days. Tardive dyskinesia: months to years.

questions.q: Lip-smacking and worm-like tongue movements are signs of:
questions.explain: Also called 'fly-catching' tongue movements.

questions.q: Compulsive, repetitive motions with agitation describe:
questions.explain: Akathisia is restlessness and inability to sit still.

questions.q: The toxic metabolite of acetaminophen that causes hepatocyte necrosis is:
questions.explain: CYP2E1 converts a small fraction of APAP to NAPQI. Glutathione normally detoxifies it.

questions.q: Chemotherapy agents that injure DNA and may cause mutagenic or carcinogenic effects show:
questions.explain: Genotoxic effects come from ionizing radiation, environmental chemicals and chemotherapy.

questions.q: Type I hypersensitivity is mediated by:
questions.explain: IgE on mast cells and basophils; onset within 1 hour; e.g. anaphylaxis.

questions.q: Hemolytic anemia is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
questions.explain: Type II is IgG/IgM cytotoxic, onset hours to days.

questions.q: Serum sickness and SLE are examples of:
questions.explain: Immune complex mediated, onset 1-3 weeks.

questions.q: Rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome are examples of:
questions.explain: Type IV takes days to weeks.

questions.q: Which hypersensitivity type has the fastest onset?
questions.explain: Type I occurs within 1 hour.

questions.q: Histamine released in type I reactions causes:
questions.explain: Histamine causes vasodilation, increased permeability, bronchoconstriction, swelling and more gastric acid.

questions.q: Idiosyncrasy is:
options: An abnormal reactivity to a chemical that is peculiar to a given individual
An immune reaction mediated by IgE
questions.explain: Example in the lecture: primaquine causing hemolytic anemia in susceptible individuals.

questions.q: Which is NOT a level of drug-drug interaction in the lecture?
questions.explain: The five are absorption, protein binding, metabolism, receptor binding and therapeutic action.

questions.q: Ranitidine can increase absorption of basic drugs such as triazolam because it:
questions.explain: H2 blockers reduce acid and raise gastric pH.

questions.q: A second drug with higher protein affinity displaces the first drug. What happens to the first drug?
questions.explain: Free drug is the active fraction, so toxicity can rise.

questions.q: Which drug is NOT listed as highly protein bound?
questions.explain: Aspirin, barbiturates, phenytoin, sulfonamides, valproic acid and warfarin are listed.

questions.q: Ethanol is a potent inducer of:
questions.explain: This increases NAPQI formation from acetaminophen.

questions.q: Buprenorphine is useful in opioid addiction because it is:
options: A partial agonist/antagonist with very high receptor affinity
questions.explain: It blocks the euphoria from other narcotics.

questions.q: Which are the three kinds of interaction of therapeutic action?
questions.explain: Shown on the isobologram.

questions.q: Which are the types of antagonism listed?
questions.explain: Function (physiological), chemical, dispositional and receptor antagonism.

questions.q: EDTA binding metal ions such as lead is what type of antagonism?
questions.explain: A chelator directly reacts with the metal to form a stable water-soluble complex.

questions.q: An antagonist that cannot be overcome by adding more agonist is:
questions.explain: Noncompetitive antagonism is unsurmountable.

questions.q: Medication errors are how much more common than adverse drug reactions?
questions.explain: This is why the five rights matter.

questions.q: Which is one of the five rights of safe medication?
questions.explain: Right drug, patient, dose, route and time.

questions.q: A passive poisoning prevention strategy:
options: Needs no behavior change, e.g. child-resistant packaging
questions.explain: Active strategies need sustained adaptation by the person.

questions.q: In the ABCDE of poisoning, D stands for:
questions.explain: A airway, B breathing, C circulation, D disability, E exposure (toxidrome).

questions.q: The first step in decontamination is to:
questions.explain: Wash eyes and skin copiously; GI decontamination comes after.

questions.q: Antidote for acetaminophen poisoning:
questions.explain: It replenishes glutathione.

questions.q: Antidote for organophosphate and carbamate pesticide poisoning:
questions.explain: Atropine blocks muscarinic effects; pralidoxime reactivates AChE for organophosphates.

questions.q: Antidote for opioid poisoning:
questions.explain: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist.

questions.q: Antidote for benzodiazepine poisoning:
questions.explain: Flumazenil blocks the benzodiazepine site.

questions.q: Antidote for iron poisoning:
questions.explain: Deferoxamine chelates iron.

questions.q: Antidote for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning:
questions.explain: They inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase.

questions.q: Antidote for coumarin (warfarin) toxicity:
questions.explain: Vitamin K1 (phytonadione) restores clotting factors.

questions.q: Antidote for methotrexate toxicity:
questions.explain: Leucovorin calcium rescues folate-dependent cells.

questions.q: Antidote for beta-blocker overdose:
questions.explain: Glucagon hydrochloride is listed for beta-adrenergic antagonists.

questions.q: Isoniazid-induced seizures are treated with:
questions.explain: Pyridoxine hydrochloride is the antidote.

questions.q: Cyanide poisoning is treated with:
questions.explain: Both are listed antidotes for cyanide.

questions.q: Methemoglobinemia is treated with:
questions.explain: Methylene blue is the listed antidote.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with:
questions.explain: Listed in the antidote table.

questions.q: Digoxin toxicity (cardiac glycosides) is treated with:
questions.explain: An antibody fragment binds digoxin.

questions.q: Malignant hyperthermia is treated with:
questions.explain: Bromocriptine is for neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.q: Drug-induced dystonia is treated with:
questions.explain: Both are listed antidotes.

questions.q: Lead poisoning can be treated with:
questions.explain: They are chelating agents.

topics.name: 2 · Drug Metabolism
topics.notes: Phase 1 (CYPs) = oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; adds functional groups. Phase 2 = conjugation; improves water solubility. Phase 3 = transport (ABC transporters). CYP3A4 handles over 50% of drugs.

questions.q: Xenobiotics are:
questions.explain: Drugs use the same enzymes and transporters used for dietary constituents.

questions.q: Phase 1 reactions include:
questions.explain: They introduce functional groups such as -OH, -COOH, -SH, -O- or NH2.

questions.q: Phase 2 reactions are called:
questions.explain: Phase 2 attaches a polar group to make the metabolite more water soluble.

questions.q: What is the main effect of phase 2 metabolism?
questions.explain: This helps excretion in urine or bile.

questions.q: Phase 1 usually does what to a drug's biological properties?
options: Dramatically alters them (inactivation) but adds little water solubility
questions.explain: The 4-hydroxyphenytoin example is only slightly soluble.

questions.q: Phase 3 of hepatic drug metabolism is:
questions.explain: Followed by excretion in urine or bile.

questions.q: CYP enzymes are:
questions.explain: Heme is bound noncovalently to a polypeptide chain.

questions.q: In CYP3A4, what does the '3' represent?
questions.explain: 3 = family, A = subfamily, 4 = gene.

questions.q: Which CYP metabolizes over 50% of drugs?
questions.explain: CYP3A4/5 is the biggest slice of phase 1 metabolism.

questions.q: The most active CYPs for drug metabolism are in:
questions.explain: Families 1, 2 and 3 are the most important for metabolism.

questions.q: CYP19 (aromatase) is inhibited by:
questions.explain: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens.

questions.q: Which is a CYP inducer?
questions.explain: Inducers: barbiturates, St. John's wort, carbamazepine, rifampin, chronic alcohol, phenytoin, griseofulvin, phenobarbital, sulfonylureas.

questions.q: Which is a CYP inhibitor?
questions.explain: Inhibitors include valproate, isoniazid, cimetidine, ketoconazole, fluconazole, erythromycin, omeprazole, grapefruit juice.

questions.q: St. John's wort affects CYP3A4 substrates by:
options: Inducing the enzyme so they are metabolized faster
questions.explain: Lower drug levels result.

questions.q: Which phase 1 enzyme family is a minor contributor and gives benign products?
questions.explain: FMO3 is the most abundant; it metabolizes nicotine, cimetidine, ranitidine, clozapine and itopride.

questions.q: UGT enzymes transfer which group?
questions.explain: This forms glucuronides.

questions.q: UGT1A1 is responsible for glucuronidation of:
questions.explain: Defects cause Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes.

questions.q: Sulfation uses which sulfate donor?
questions.explain: SULT enzymes use PAPS.

questions.q: SULT2A1 in the fetal adrenal produces DHEA sulfate (DHEAS), needed for:
questions.explain: Needed in the second half of pregnancy.

questions.q: Glutathione is a tripeptide of:
questions.explain: Its thiol group on cysteine binds electrophiles.

questions.q: In acetaminophen overdose, N-acetylcysteine helps by:
questions.explain: Glutathione conjugation converts NAPQI to non-toxic metabolites.

questions.q: N-acetyltransferases metabolize drugs containing:
options: An aromatic amine or hydrazine group
questions.explain: Example: isoniazid.

questions.q: The acetylator phenotype is most relevant to which drug?
questions.explain: Slow acetylators have higher isoniazid levels.

questions.q: Methylation uses which methyl donor?
questions.explain: It can be O-, N- or S-methylation.

questions.q: Which enzyme methylates catecholamines like norepinephrine?
questions.explain: COMT produces normetanephrine, metanephrine and methoxytyramine.

questions.q: TPMT is important in the metabolism of:
questions.explain: TPMT methylates 6-MP to an inactive metabolite.

topics.name: 3 · Autonomics Part 1
topics.notes: ANS: sympathetic = fight or flight; parasympathetic = rest and digest. ACh is the transmitter at all autonomic ganglia, parasympathetic endings and the NMJ. Cholinergic drugs can be direct (muscarinic, nicotinic) or indirect (AChE inhibitors).

questions.q: The ANS controls:
options: Involuntary, unconscious regulation of internal functions
questions.explain: It has sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

questions.q: The sympathetic division is best known for:
questions.explain: Parasympathetic is rest and digest.

questions.q: Anticholinergic toxicity: 'HOT as a hare, DRY as a bone, RED as a beet' - what does 'BLIND as a bat' mean?
questions.explain: Also MAD as a hatter (CNS toxicity).

questions.q: ACh is the primary transmitter at:
options: All autonomic ganglia, parasympathetic endings and the NMJ
questions.explain: It is also the exception at eccrine sweat glands (sympathetic but cholinergic).

questions.q: Which drug blocks the choline transporter (CHT)?
questions.explain: CHT is a Na+/choline symporter.

questions.q: Vesamicol blocks:
questions.explain: ACh storage in vesicles.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh:
questions.explain: Release needs Ca2+ and VAMP/SNARE proteins.

questions.q: AChE degrades ACh into:
questions.explain: Choline is recycled by CHT.

questions.q: Which synthesizes ACh?
questions.explain: ChAT combines choline and acetyl CoA.

questions.q: Which direct agonist activates both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors and is used as a miotic eye drop?
questions.explain: Choline esters like bethanechol are muscarinic only.

questions.q: Bethanechol is used for:
questions.explain: It is a nonselective muscarinic choline ester.

questions.q: Methacholine is used to:
questions.explain: A challenge test for airway hyperreactivity.

questions.q: Pilocarpine is an M3-selective alkaloid used for:
questions.explain: It stimulates lacrimal and salivary secretion. Most common side effect: sweating.

questions.q: Muscarinic toxicity is treated with:
questions.explain: A muscarinic antagonist.

questions.q: Edrophonium is a short-acting AChE inhibitor used as:
options: Bedside diagnostic tool for myasthenia gravis
questions.explain: Reversibly binds AChE.

questions.q: Neostigmine and pyridostigmine are used to treat:
questions.explain: They are carbamates (-stigmines).

questions.q: Which AChE inhibitor enters the CNS and fixes atropine overdose?
questions.explain: Neostigmine does not cross the BBB well.

questions.q: Parathion and malathion are:
questions.explain: Used as pesticides; very long acting.

questions.q: Tabun, sarin and soman are:
questions.explain: Very long-acting AChE inhibitors.

questions.q: Which drugs treat Alzheimer dementia by inhibiting AChE?
questions.explain: Cholinergic neuron deficiency is found in Alzheimer dementia.

questions.q: Nicotine (full agonist) and varenicline (partial agonist) are used for:
questions.explain: They act on neuronal and muscular nicotinic receptors.

questions.q: Succinylcholine is:
questions.explain: It is a nicotinic muscular (Nm) agonist.

topics.name: 4 · Autonomics Part 2
topics.notes: Antimuscarinics (atropine prototype), nicotinic blockers, then adrenergic pharmacology: catecholamine synthesis, receptors, sympathomimetics and sympatholytics.

questions.q: The prototype muscarinic antagonist is:
questions.explain: It blocks ALL muscarinic receptors.

questions.q: The first choice for organophosphate poisoning is:
questions.explain: It counters excess muscarinic stimulation.

questions.q: Which is used for acute asthma and COPD?
questions.explain: Tiotropium has the longest half-life.

questions.q: Scopolamine is mainly used for:
questions.explain: It crosses the BBB better than atropine.

questions.q: Oxybutynin is used for:
questions.explain: An M3 blocker.

questions.q: Pirenzepine is an M1-selective blocker used for:
questions.explain: It decreases gastric acid secretion.

questions.q: Hexamethonium is a:
questions.explain: Formerly used for hypertension; obsolete.

questions.q: Tubocurarine, pancuronium, atracurium and vecuronium are used for:
questions.explain: They are Nm blockers.

questions.q: The primary neurotransmitter of sympathetic postganglionic fibers is:
questions.explain: Exception: eccrine sweat glands use ACh.

questions.q: The rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis is:
options: Tyrosine to L-DOPA by tyrosine hydroxylase
questions.explain: Metyrosine inhibits it.

questions.q: Reserpine blocks:
questions.explain: Catecholamine storage in vesicles.

questions.q: Guanethidine inhibits:
questions.explain: Amphetamines, ephedrine and tyramine promote release.

questions.q: Cocaine and tricyclic antidepressants block:
questions.explain: This prolongs catecholamine action.

questions.q: First-line drug in septic shock:
questions.explain: It raises total peripheral resistance.

questions.q: Epinephrine is used for:
questions.explain: It has B1 = B2 > alpha activity.

questions.q: Low-dose dopamine acts on:
questions.explain: Mid dose: B1; high dose: alpha-1.

questions.q: Phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine and oxymetazoline are used as:
questions.explain: Alpha-1 agonists cause nasal vasoconstriction.

questions.q: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist used for:
questions.explain: Off-label: ADHD and Tourette.

questions.q: Methyldopa is used for:
questions.explain: An alpha-2 agonist.

questions.q: Dobutamine is a B1 agonist used for:
options: Cardiogenic shock and cardiac stress testing
questions.explain: It increases cardiac contractility.

questions.q: Salbutamol, terbutaline and isoxsuprine are:
options: Beta-2 agonists for asthma and tocolysis
questions.explain: Side effects: tachycardia, tremors, nervousness.

questions.q: Which is a reversible nonselective alpha blocker used before pheochromocytoma surgery?
questions.explain: Phenoxybenzamine is the irreversible one.

questions.q: Alpha-1 blockers (-zosins) are used for:
questions.explain: Side effect: orthostatic hypotension. Tamsulosin is the most prostate-selective.

questions.q: Which beta blocker is the shortest acting and given IV?
questions.explain: A B1-selective blocker.

questions.q: Propranolol is a:
questions.explain: Also used for hyperthyroidism and migraine prophylaxis.

questions.q: Which are B1-selective beta blockers?
questions.explain: Nonselective: propranolol, pindolol, timolol, labetalol, carvedilol.

topics.name: 5 · Hormones and Diabetes
topics.notes: Insulin (beta cells) lowers glucose; glucagon (alpha cells) raises it. T1DM = beta-cell destruction; T2DM = insulin resistance with relative deficiency. Know the drug classes, mechanisms and key side effects.

questions.q: Endocrine glands secrete their products:
questions.explain: Exocrine glands secrete into ducts.

questions.q: About 99% of the pancreas is made of:
questions.explain: Islets of Langerhans are scattered among acini.

questions.q: Which islet cell makes insulin (about 70%)?
questions.explain: Alpha 17% glucagon; delta 7% somatostatin; F cells pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.q: Alpha cells secrete:
questions.explain: Glucagon is the main hormone in the fasting state.

questions.q: Delta cells secrete:
questions.explain: 7% of islet cells.

questions.q: Insulin has two chains linked by disulfide bridges. These are:
questions.explain: Proinsulin also contains C-peptide.

questions.q: Type 1 DM is characterized by:
options: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency
questions.explain: Usually diagnosed before age 30; insulin-dependent.

questions.q: Type 2 DM is characterized by:
options: Tissue resistance to insulin with relative deficiency of secretion
questions.explain: It may initially be controlled with diet, exercise and oral agents.

questions.q: HbA1c reflects glucose control over about:
questions.explain: A longer-term marker than fingerstick glucose.

questions.q: Which is a diabetic complication?
questions.explain: Microvascular complications.

questions.q: Which insulin is rapid-acting?
questions.explain: Regular is short-acting; NPH is intermediate; glargine, detemir, degludec are long-acting.

questions.q: The most common side effect of insulin is:
questions.explain: Teach patients and family the signs of hypoglycemia.

questions.q: Which insulin can be used IV in emergencies?
questions.explain: It is short-acting.

questions.q: Sulfonylureas increase insulin release by:
options: Inhibiting efflux of potassium ions (closing K-ATP channels)
questions.explain: Second-generation: glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride, gliclazide.

questions.q: The major side effect of gliclazide is:
questions.explain: Sulfonylureas are secretagogues.

questions.q: Meglitinides (repaglinide, mitiglinide) differ from sulfonylureas by:
options: Faster onset, shorter duration, taken before meals
questions.explain: They control postprandial glucose.

questions.q: First-line therapy in type 2 DM:
questions.explain: A biguanide.

questions.q: Metformin works mainly by:
options: Activating AMPK to reduce hepatic glucose production
questions.explain: Also used in PCOS.

questions.q: Which are side effects of metformin?
options: GI upset, vitamin B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis
questions.explain: GI effects are most common.

questions.q: Pioglitazone and rosiglitazone work as ligands of:
questions.explain: These are thiazolidinediones.

questions.q: Which is a side effect of thiazolidinediones?
options: Fluid retention (heart failure), bone loss, weight gain
questions.explain: Also edema and anemia.

questions.q: Exenatide, semaglutide and liraglutide are:
questions.explain: They cause weight loss; side effects are GI disturbances and acute pancreatitis.

questions.q: Sitagliptin, saxagliptin and linagliptin are:
questions.explain: Side effects: headache, nasopharyngitis, URTI.

questions.q: Acarbose and miglitol:
options: Delay carbohydrate digestion, reducing post-meal glucose
questions.explain: Side effects: flatulence, diarrhea, abdominal pain. No effect on fasting glucose.

questions.q: Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin cause:
questions.explain: Side effects: genital and urinary tract infections.

questions.q: Target HbA1c for most patients:
questions.explain: 8% is acceptable for elderly frail patients.

questions.q: Target pre-meal glucose:
questions.explain: 5-7.2 mmol/L.

questions.q: Target 2-hour postprandial glucose:
questions.explain: The 1-hour target is less than 180 mg/dL.

questions.q: Blood pressure target in diabetes (lecture):
questions.explain: Part of the glycemic and BP targets.

questions.q: Estimated daily insulin units needed:
questions.explain: For type 1 DM, given as at least 3-4 injections daily.

questions.q: A diet recommended for diabetes:
options: Mediterranean-style, limiting carbohydrates, using monounsaturated fats
questions.explain: Olive oil, canola oil, nuts and avocados.

topics.name: 6 · Antihypertensive Drugs
topics.notes: BP = CO x SVR; CO = HR x SV. Drug classes: diuretics, sympatholytics, vasodilators, drugs blocking angiotensin (ACE inhibitors, ARBs), plus calcium channel blockers.

questions.q: Blood pressure equals:
options: Cardiac output x systemic vascular resistance
questions.explain: BP = CO x SVR, and CO = HR x SV.

questions.q: Cardiac output equals:
questions.explain: CO = HR x SV.

questions.q: Primary (essential) hypertension is:
options: Hypertension due to kidney disease only
questions.explain: Secondary hypertension has a specific etiology.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four antihypertensive drug groups in the lecture?
questions.explain: The fourth group blocks production or action of angiotensin.

questions.q: Diuretics lower BP mainly by:
questions.explain: They lower BP by about 10-15 mmHg in most patients.

questions.q: Loop diuretics inhibit:
options: NKCC2 (Na/K/Cl cotransporter) in the thick ascending limb
questions.explain: Prototypes: furosemide and ethacrynic acid; also bumetanide and torsemide.

questions.q: Which is a loop diuretic?
questions.explain: Furosemide is the prototype.

questions.q: Loop diuretics are used for:
options: Acute pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, acute renal failure
questions.explain: They are strong diuretics for edematous conditions.

questions.q: A characteristic toxicity of loop diuretics:
questions.explain: Also allergic reactions.

questions.q: Thiazide diuretics block:
options: The Na/Cl cotransporter (NCC) in the distal convoluted tubule
questions.explain: The prototype is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ).

questions.q: Thiazide toxicities include:
questions.explain: Also allergic reactions.

questions.q: Spironolactone and eplerenone are:
questions.explain: They prevent K+ secretion in the collecting tubules.

questions.q: Amiloride and triamterene act by:
questions.explain: Also potassium-sparing.

questions.q: Toxicity of potassium-sparing diuretics:
questions.explain: Uses: hyperaldosteronism and heart failure.

questions.q: Which is an oral vasodilator for hypertension?
questions.explain: Parenteral vasodilators: nitroprusside and fenoldopam.

questions.q: Parenteral vasodilators in the lecture:
questions.explain: They are used for severe hypertension.

questions.q: Which are non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers?
questions.explain: Dihydropyridines: amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine, nicardipine.

questions.q: Calcium channel blockers lower BP by:
options: Inhibiting Ca2+ influx into arterial smooth muscle cells
questions.explain: This causes vasodilation.

questions.q: Which sympatholytic drugs are listed?
questions.explain: Also phentolamine and phenoxybenzamine.

questions.q: ACE inhibitors work by:
options: Blocking conversion of angiotensin I to II and inactivating bradykinin
questions.explain: Examples: captopril, enalapril, ramipril.

questions.q: Which is an ACE inhibitor?
questions.explain: The -pril drugs are ACE inhibitors.

questions.q: ACE inhibitors are preferred in chronic kidney disease because they:
options: Reduce proteinuria and stabilize renal function
questions.explain: Especially useful in diabetes.

questions.q: Toxicities of ACE inhibitors:
questions.explain: Both are linked to increased bradykinin.

questions.q: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in:
questions.explain: They can harm the fetus.

questions.q: ARBs (losartan, valsartan, candesartan, irbesartan, telmisartan) block:
questions.explain: The -sartans.

questions.q: Compared with ACE inhibitors, ARBs:
options: Do not affect bradykinin, so cough is less likely
questions.explain: ARBs are more selective blockers of angiotensin effects.
